blocks.text: Paul contrasts his own weakness, fear, and trembling with rhetorical superiority, directing attention instead to the proclaimed crucified Christ and to God’s power. The contrast challenges prestige-based persuasion, but it does not make poor communication, manipulation, or inaccessible speech into virtues.

The “mystery” and hidden wisdom of verses 6–16 are presented as God’s wisdom made known through the Spirit, not as elitist secret knowledge. The passage contrasts this wisdom with that of the rulers of the age and describes spiritual reception and discernment; its claims remain bounded by the crucified Christ and the chapter’s argument, rather than granting immunity from thoughtful judgment.

The surrounding discussion distinguishes rhetorical weakness and the apparent weakness of the crucified Messiah from bodily impairment, illness, injury, persecution, poverty, or imprisonment. These experiences may overlap, but they are not interchangeable. The letter locates its reversal of conventional power and status in the proclamation of the cross and the formation of the community, not in requiring vulnerable people to remain powerless.

sections.title: Weakness and Power in the Wider Argument
